extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners and patent practitioners evaluating subject-matter eligibility (life sciences & data-processing)
extracted.subtask_description: Framework and practice guidance for analyzing whether patent claims are directed to statutory subject matter under the Alice/Mayo/2019 PEG framework, with examples in life sciences and data-processing. Focuses on claim interpretation, whether claims recite judicial exceptions, integration into a practical application, and whether claims amount to significantly more than an exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim interpretation (broadest reasonable interpretation / BRI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the broadest reasonable interpretation, claim terms are presumed to have their plain meaning consistent with the specification as interpreted by one of ordinary skill in the art; preambles do not necessarily add limitations; wherein/contingent clauses cannot be disregarded; system claims require the structure for performing a recited function to be present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use MPEP 2111. Consider the specification to construe terms (e.g., memory, display, processor are known classes of structures). Contingent limitations in system and process claims must be given weight (see MPEP 2111.04(II)). The same claim interpretation must be used across eligibility, definiteness, novelty, obviousness, written description analyses. Examples: wherein clauses carrying patentable weight; contingent step (d) producing multiple embodiments under the BRI—anticipation analysis need only target one embodiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1 — Statutory category determination
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the claim falls within any statutory category (process, machine, manufacture, composition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply MPEP 2106.03. Example: a claim reciting memory, display, and processor is a machine; a claim reciting an analyzing step is a process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A Prong One — Does the claim recite a judicial exception?
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim 'recites' a judicial exception (abstract idea, mental process, law of nature, natural phenomenon) — i.e., whether the exception is 'set forth' or described in the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use MPEP 2106.04(II) and 2019 PEG guidance. Examples: comparing/analysis/evaluation limitations (e.g., comparing current animal behavior to past behavior to identify aberrance) are mental processes and fall within the abstract idea/mental process grouping. If no nature-based product limitations are present, the 'markedly different characteristics' analysis need not be performed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine recited judicial exceptions into a single abstract idea when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: When a series of steps each recite judicial exceptions, treat the recited exceptions in combination as a single abstract idea for purposes of further eligibility analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow MPEP 2106.04 and 2106.05(II). Example: limitations (a) and (b) (comparing and analyzing animal-specific information) are combined and treated as one abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A Prong Two — Integration into a practical application
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify additional elements beyond the judicial exception and evaluate whether those elements individually or in combination integrate the exception into a practical application (i.e., whether the claim as a whole applies the exception in a meaningful, practical way).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform a two-part evaluation: (a) identify additional elements beyond the judicial exception and (b) evaluate whether those elements integrate the exception into a practical application (2019 PEG Section III(A)(2)). Generic recitations of memory, display, and processor typically do not integrate. Elements that use information from the exception to control physical equipment (e.g., operating a feed dispenser or sorting gate) may be 'other meaningful limitations' that integrate the exception and render the claim directed to a practical application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insignificant extra-solution activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether additional elements represent mere data gathering or nominal/tangential additions to the claim that are insignificant to solving the asserted technical problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At Step 2A Prong Two, exclude consideration of whether such elements are well-understood or conventional. Examples of insignificant extra-solution activity include high-level data gathering (livestock interface obtaining animal-specific information), generic presentation of results (displaying analyzed data), or printing a generated menu. Cite MPEP 2106.05(g) and cases such as Electric Power Group and Ameranth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B — Significantly more / inventive concept analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the recited judicial exception — i.e., whether any additional element or combination adds an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Re-evaluate elements previously deemed 'insignificant extra-solution activity' with regard to whether those elements are well-known or routine; if they are well-known, they cannot supply an inventive concept. Mere instructions to apply an exception on a computer (memory/display/processor) generally do not supply 'significantly more.' Use MPEP 2106.05 and relevant Federal Circuit case law (e.g., Credit Acceptance, Trading Technologies, FairWarning).

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of generic computer components
rubrics_metrics.description: Recitation of generic computer components (e.g., processor, memory, display) does not negate the mental nature of claim limitations when the computer is merely used as a tool to perform the mental process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generic computer hardware recited at a high level is often treated as 'mere instructions to apply the judicial exception on a computer' and does not improve computer functionality. Cite Alice, Credit Acceptance, and related MPEP discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field-of-use / token limitation does not make an abstract idea patent eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations that merely link the claim to a particular field (e.g., livestock management) are token field-of-use restrictions and do not integrate an abstract idea into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy to Bilski: identifying participants or application area without technical improvement does not make the claim eligible (MPEP 2106.05(h)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Automation of human mental processes is insufficient absent technical improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Automating mental processes using generic computer components, even if improving convenience or daily life, does not constitute an improvement to computer functionality or other technology and thus does not render the claim eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite cases where improved speed or convenience from a general-purpose computer was insufficient (e.g., Credit Acceptance, Trading Technologies, FairWarning, Trading Technologies Int'l v. IBG). The claim must change the computer or other technology in a meaningful way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular treatment or prophylaxis consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim invokes the 'particular treatment or prophylaxis' consideration only if it affirmatively recites an action that effects a particular treatment or prophylaxis for a disease or medical condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim only detects a condition but does not affirmatively perform the treatment (e.g., does not actually dispense therapeutics), the treatment/prophylaxis consideration does not apply (see practice note referencing Ino Therapeutics). However, combining detection with automatic control of equipment to effect treatment may invoke the 'other meaningful limitation' consideration and support eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice note for drafting / issuing rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: When issuing a rejection under the eligibility framework, identify the specific limitations that embody the judicial exception and explain why they are abstract; explain why the additional elements do not integrate the exception into a practical application or amount to significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite supportive court decisions where appropriate (e.g., CyberSource, University of Utah Research Foundation v. Ambry Genetics, Electric Power Group). Explain which elements are insignificant extra-solution activity and whether any element adds a meaningful limitation or inventive concept. Provide clear linkage to the claim language (e.g., point to limitations (a) and (b)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Contingent claim limitations and embodiment breadth under BRI
rubrics_metrics.description: Contingent limitations create alternative embodiments under the broadest reasonable interpretation; the claim may encompass multiple distinct embodiments and a prior art reference need only teach one embodiment to anticipate the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP 2111.04(II). Example: a contingent step that routes animals in certain conditions creates embodiments where only one or both contingent actions occur; all such embodiments are encompassed by the claim under BRI and must be considered for novelty/anticipation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconsideration of 'insignificant extra-solution activity' at Step 2B with respect to conventionality
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements deemed insignificant at Step 2A Prong Two must be re-evaluated at Step 2B to determine whether they are well-understood, routine, or conventional; if so, they cannot supply an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow 2019 PEG Section III(B) and MPEP 2106.05(g). Example: a livestock interface that is mere data gathering and disclosed in the specification as well-known remains insignificant at Step 2B and thus does not provide 'significantly more.'
